Free the Nipple

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.. a bare-breasted fight for equal rights

Unique Selling Point:
A campaign for equal rights for women that uses a rather peculiar metaphor to bring the message home.

Summary:
Free the Nipple is a gender equality campaign named after Lina Esco's 2014/15 film Free the Nipple. The campaign argues that women and men should be granted the same freedom, and protection, under the law. The movement aims to advance gender equality and to oppose sexual objectification.

Further information:
Actress Lina Esco wanted to make a difference in the world all her life. Growing up dirt poor in Florida she vowed to one day campaign for equal rights for women in the US because she witnessed the struggles her mother had. To this day in the US women earn much less than men for equal work, they have glass ceilings in business and fewer opportunities in the corporate world. Women are earning the majority of undergraduate and graduate degrees (60 percent), while at the same time, women make up the majority of the poor in America. Surprisingly the U.S. Constitution does not guarantee equal rights for women. Since 1923, activists have been trying to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), which states, “Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.” However, ERA has never been passed and is not part of the Constitution. In addition, aspects of women's lives are also treated differently in many states in the US. For example, in Louisiana a woman can be arrested and jailed for breastfeeding in public. Lina had been acutely aware of the lack of equal rights for women and decided to put that in the spotlight, she decided on a novel approach and decided to use a metaphor that would have wide public impact. She decided on the nipple. In the US today, the nipples of men, that are no different from that of women can be sees and displayed in public, but female nipples not. They are considered indecent. This freedom men have in going topless was not always there. Until the 1930's men were prohibited from showing their nipples and were forced to wear swimwear that covered their nipples. They could be fined or jailed if they did not abide by the law. However, an organised protest in New York changed this for men. It was never extended to women. In this Lina saw a prime example of the lack of equal rights of women and decided to make a film called "Free the Nipple". She easily got money, shot it in New York City and completed the film in 2013. However, no film festival would take the film and she had trouble with distributors. While this was going on, word of the film came out and surprisingly a whole movement called "Free the Nipple" stared. The idea resonated with men and women across the US and became a social movement with annual celebrations and events across the country. This triggered interest in the film and it was released in 2014/15.

American taboos surrounding the female nipple are further enforced by many social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram which prohibit any and all "graphic content" that pictures a woman's areola. Instagram's Community Guideline's demands of its users, "Keep your clothes on." However, this rule seems only to apply to images that contain women's nipples as they are promptly removed by Instagram unless the areola itself is covered. In contrast, photos featuring topless men are generally not subject to this regulation. Chelsea Handler, Miley Cyrus, Rihanna and Scout Willis have each received backlash from Instagram for sharing photos of their chests exposed. Willow Smith also had a post removed because it pictured her wearing a shirt with a pair of women's nipples printed on it, though the shirt itself was fairly conservative in cut. Some have even gone so far as to photoshop male nipples onto their pictures posted on Instagram in order to cover their female nipples. This is mostly used to make the comparison between the two and censorship. When explaining the need to remove nudity, Instagram's CEO Kevin Systrom blamed the rating system of Apple's app store. Eliminating online censorship of Free the Nipple posts is one of the goals of the movement. Censorship, and especially that of social media sites, exacerbates the problem that social movements, primarily those considered taboo, run into, which is spreading the message. The use of social media like Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram, has greatly improved activists ability to spread their message in the last decade, making it easier to create a collective identity. Free the Nipple activists need ICT's in their repertoire because social media shares lead to accelerated pluralism, which can then lead to the spillover effect, which can be seen in the Occupy Wall Street and Arab Spring movements. The spillover into the public sphere is what social movement activists hope for. In 2015, the campaign received attention in Iceland and was supported by MP Björt Ólafsdottir, who posted a topless photo of herself, in solidarity with a teenage activist who had received harassment for doing the same.

Lina speaks exceptionally well, is articulate and passionate about her ideal for equal rights for women. We also have permission to use the film.

The Free the Nipple website says:
FREE THE NIPPLE IS A GLOBAL CAMPAIGN OF CHANGE, FOCUSED ON THE EQUALITY, EMPOWERMENT, AND FREEDOM OF ALL HUMAN BEINGS. FREE THE NIPPLE HAS BECOME A PREMIERE VOICE FOR GENDER EQUALITY, UTILIZING ALL FORMS OF MODERN MEDIA, TO RAISE AWARENESS AND EFFECT CHANGE ON VARIOUS SOCIAL ISSUES, AND INJUSTICES.

WE BELIEVE THAT ALL HUMAN BEINGS ARE CREATED EQUAL.

WE BELIEVE THAT THE TIME FOR CHANGE IS NOW.

WE BELIEVE THAT TOGETHER, THROUGH ONE UNIFIED VOICE, WE CAN AFFECT CHANGE GLOBALLY.

OUR MISSION:

FREE THE NIPPLE IS A GLOBAL PLATFORM FOR CHANGE IN THE WORLD.

WE BELIEVE THAT AS HUMAN BEINGS, WE SHOULD ALL BE TREATED EQUALLY.

WE ARE A GLOBAL MOVEMENT OF EQUALITY, EMPOWERMENT AND FREEDOM.

WE ARE A MOVEMENT OF CHANGE.

Press Release:


Free the Nipple
An improbable body part has become a global symbol of the bare-breasted fight for equality between men and women: the nipple. Carte Blanche meets Lina Esco, the charismatic founder of the controversial Free the Nipple Campaign and finds out how her drive to do something disruptive and change the way people think about gender equality caused chaos on New York streets.


Script:


V/O:
Some call it the biggest cover-up from the last 100 years. These women are all obviously hiding something. Something we are not allowed to see. These shrouded assets are their nipples.

But topless men seem to be OK. Their nipples can be seen.

But if this woman gets her way, women’s nipples will soon be as free as men’s. Her name is Lina Esco and she started a movement aptly called Free the Nipple.

But liberating nipples is not the main issue. The nipple is merely a metaphor for a much larger issue: gender equality.
Lina:
If I would have made a movie and a movement called equality and nobody was going topless, no one would be talking about this.
V/O:
But people are talking about it. And all over the US women are starting to bare their breasts. But how does public nudity advance women’s rights?
Lina:
Free the Nipple is not about nudity, it’s about equality. It is not about going topless. This is about a much bigger conversation which is equality. This is what we had to do in order to have that platform for people to speak about equality.
V/O:
Women have historically bared their breasts during protests such as those by American Animal Rights Organisation PETA against animal abuse. In South Africa three Wits students recently bared their breasts during a Fees must fall protest to show their intolerance of violence.

But Lina wants to protest gender inequality across the board. She wants to bring female nipples out into the open permanently as a lasting reminder of the issue. She’s even produced a feature film in the topic.
LINK
The film tells the story of a group of young women in New York who start to go topless to raise awareness about the many inequalities between men and women.
V/O:
Every country grapples with inequality in some sense. But few people know that the US Constitution does not explicitly guarantee equal rights for women.

Back in nineteen twenty three an Equal Rights Amendment or ERA was proposed, giving all citizens equal rights irrespective of their sex. But the ERA has never been ratified—leaving dire consequences for women in the US.
Lina:
In America there is a lot of inequality and the victims that are falling into this the most are women.
V/O:
Inequalities are apparent throughout American society.
LINK:
Only 4,2% of the CEO’s of America’s top 500 companies are female.
V/O:
American women are nearly twice as likely as men to retire in poverty despite the fact that they earn sixty percent of University degrees. Inequality seems to touch every area of life.
Lina:
Equal pay, there is no equal pay in America. You know, women are still getting paid 78c for every dollar a man makes. And we are not even mentioning minorities which is 65 c or less.
V/O:
American women also experience that their personal issues are not really taken seriously. Though mothers of newborns are guaranteed paid maternity leave in a hundred and eighty eight countries, this isn’t the case in the US.

And women are also banned from breastfeeding in public in many states and jurisdictions.
As a teenager Lina became intensely aware of these limitations.
Lina:
And the more I started researching about women’s rights, I felt more and more compelled to bring the female voice back again in this generation.
V/O:
When she was 20 Lina managed to break into film and television landing a role on the CSI series. This was followed by roles in films such as London and LOL. Both this exposure and the network of celebrities she came to know gave her an opportunity to seriously start looking for ways to advance the equality conversation in the US.
Lina:
I have been a rebel pretty much since I was really young and everything that I do in my life somehow has to push the boundaries.
LINK:
She started to look for an attention-grabbing vehicle to address the inequalities between male and female in a unique way.
V/O:
And she found this in highlighting discrimination in the way in which the public display of female and male nipples is handled.

And, while men are these days allowed to display their nipples, to her surprise Lina discovered that this was not always the case.
Lina:
A lot of people don’t know this bit in the early 1900’s, like back in the 1930’s, thousands of men were you know protesting because they wanted to be able to have the right to go topless.
V/O:
Men could be fined or arrested if they were topless in public and had to wear swimsuits covering everything. They did not like this and protested in all kinds of ways. Finally, in 1936 they obtained the right to go topless in public. But women did not.
Lina:
It is like if a man is going to be able to have those rights, women should be able to have those rights.
V/O:
But it did not happen. Instead women’s nipples became something obscene and shameful and had to be covered up at all times.

This approach is evident on social media.
Lina:
You can sell guns on Instagram, you can show beheadings of women on Facebook. The moment a woman shows her nipple, which is really the same as a man’s nipple, or survives breast cancer and posts a picture of herself topless, or whatever, she is banned. The nipple has become the symbol of oppression.
LINK:
It was the sexy and attention-grabbing symbol she was looking for.
V/O:
And for Lina the slogan “Free the nipple” aptly articulated the need for liberation from oppression.

When shooting began on Lina’s film, it caused upheaval on New York’s streets. It seemed that neither public bystanders nor the police were open to the scenes being acted out.
CLIP OF PREVIEW
It has been a really long, tough process trying to make it. Everybody has been trying to censor us.
V/O:
Lina would have run into similar problems in South Africa. Here public nudity and exposure of female breasts are prohibited under the Sexual Offences Act.

However, public nudity is tolerated on certain designated beaches or at pre-approved events such as the annual naked bike event in Cape Town—held in protest of our dependence on oil-. Breastfeeding in public is legal in South Africa.

Despite clashes with authorities and an unsympathetic New York City public, Lina finished her film. But she could not find a distributor for the movie – they all thought it was a porn.

This forced her to postpone the film’s release date,

But when celebrities like Scout Willis, Lena Dunham, Rihanna and Mylie Cyrus started to support the idea on social media, something unexpected happened.
LINK:
The idea of Free the Nipple resonated with people all over the US and overnight a robust social movement advocating gender equality was born.
Lina:
We get a lot of reaction and that is all that matters. I get hundreds of e-mails from girls that is 16. 17. Boys in high school, middle school, college writing papers on this. Doing debates in school with teachers about this, doing presentations, theses on this. They get it! They know this is not about going topless.
LINK:
And suddenly film distributors started to become interested. Last year the movie was released in theatres.
V/O:
Lina herself experienced a moment of liberation while making the film.
Lina:
And that was the first thing when I first was topless, was in Times Square. And when I was like running through Times Square topless and I was like “They’ve been stealing this away from us? They made us shameful for this?”
V/O:
Since the release of the film the movement has really exploded and there are regular Free the Nipple events all around the US. The main thing on the agenda at these events is gender equality.

And this unorthodox equality movement has also begun to attract a lot of attention internationally.
Lina:
Who would have thought that the nipple was going to be the Trojan horse that was going to start the conversation about equality and oppression of women around the globe?

She wants to bring female nipples out into the open permanently as a lasting reminder of the issue. She’s even produced a feature film in the topic. LINK The film tells the story of a group of young women in New York who start to go topless to raise awareness about the many inequalities between men and women. V/O: Every country grapples with inequality in some sense. But few people know that the US Constitution does not explicitly guarantee equal rights for women. Back in nineteen twenty three an Equal Rights Amendment or ERA was proposed, giving all citizens equal rights irrespective of their sex. But the ERA has never been ratified—leaving dire consequences for women in the US. Lina: In America there is a lot of inequality and the victims that are falling into this the most are women. V/O: Inequalities are apparent throughout American society. LINK: Only 4,2% of the CEO’s of America’s top 500 companies are female. V/O: American women are nearly twice as likely as men to retire in poverty despite the fact that they earn sixty percent of University degrees. Inequality seems to touch every area of life. Lina: Equal pay, there is no equal pay in America. You know, women are still getting paid 78c for every dollar a man makes. And we are not even mentioning minorities which is 65 c or less. V/O: American women also experience that their personal issues are not really taken seriously. Though mothers of newborns are guaranteed paid maternity leave in a hundred and eighty eight countries, this isn’t the case in the US. And women are also banned from breastfeeding in public in many states and jurisdictions. As a teenager Lina became intensely aware of these limitations. Lina: And the more I started researching about women’s rights, I felt more and more compelled to bring the female voice back again in this generation. V/O: When she was 20 Lina managed to break into film and television landing a role on the CSI series. This was followed by roles in films such as London and LOL. Both this exposure and the network of celebrities she came to know gave her an opportunity to seriously start looking for ways to advance the equality conversation in the US. Lina: I have been a rebel pretty much since I was really young and everything that I do in my life somehow has to push the boundaries. LINK: She started to look for an attention-grabbing vehicle to address the inequalities between male and female in a unique way. V/O: And she found this in highlighting discrimination in the way in which the public display of female and male nipples is handled. And, while men are these days allowed to display their nipples, to her surprise Lina discovered that this was not always the case. Lina: A lot of people don’t know this bit in the early 1900’s, like back in the 1930’s, thousands of men were you know protesting because they wanted to be able to have the right to go topless. V/O: Men could be fined or arrested if they were topless in public and had to wear swimsuits covering everything. They did not like this and protested in all kinds of ways. Finally, in 1936 they obtained the right to go topless in public. But women did not. Lina: It is like if a man is going to be able to have those rights, women should be able to have those rights. V/O: But it did not happen. Instead women’s nipples became something obscene and shameful and had to be covered up at all times. This approach is evident on social media. Lina: You can sell guns on Instagram, you can show beheadings of women on Facebook. The moment a woman shows her nipple, which is really the same as a man’s nipple, or survives breast cancer and posts a picture of herself topless, or whatever, she is banned. The nipple has become the symbol of oppression. LINK: It was the sexy and attention-grabbing symbol she was looking for. V/O: And for Lina the slogan “Free the nipple” aptly articulated the need for liberation from oppression. When shooting began on Lina’s film, it caused upheaval on New York’s streets. It seemed that neither public bystanders nor the police were open to the scenes being acted out. CLIP OF PREVIEW It has been a really long, tough process trying to make it. Everybody has been trying to censor us. V/O: Lina would have run into similar problems in South Africa. Here public nudity and exposure of female breasts are prohibited under the Sexual Offences Act. However, public nudity is tolerated on certain designated beaches or at pre-approved events such as the annual naked bike event in Cape Town—held in protest of our dependence on oil-. Breastfeeding in public is legal in South Africa. Despite clashes with authorities and an unsympathetic New York City public, Lina finished her film. But she could not find a distributor for the movie – they all thought it was a porn. This forced her to postpone the film’s release date, But when celebrities like Scout Willis, Lena Dunham, Rihanna and Mylie Cyrus started to support the idea on social media, something unexpected happened. LINK: The idea of Free the Nipple resonated with people all over the US and overnight a robust social movement advocating gender equality was born. Lina: We get a lot of reaction and that is all that matters. I get hundreds of e-mails from girls that is 16. 17. Boys in high school, middle school, college writing papers on this. Doing debates in school with teachers about this, doing presentations, theses on this. They get it! They know this is not about going topless. LINK: And suddenly film distributors started to become interested. Last year the movie was released in theatres. V/O: Lina herself experienced a moment of liberation while making the film. Lina: And that was the first thing when I first was topless, was in Times Square. And when I was like running through Times Square topless and I was like “They’ve been stealing this away from us? They made us shameful for this?” V/O: Since the release of the film the movement has really exploded and there are regular Free the Nipple events all around the US. The main thing on the agenda at these events is gender equality. And this unorthodox equality movement has also begun to attract a lot of attention internationally. Lina: Who would have thought that the nipple was going to be the Trojan horse that was going to start the conversation about equality and oppression of women around the globe?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): .. a bare-breasted fight for equal rights
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A campaign for equal rights for women that uses a rather peculiar metaphor to bring the message home.
metadata.Summary: Free the Nipple is a gender equality campaign named after Lina Esco's 2014/15 film Free the Nipple. The campaign argues that women and men should be granted the same freedom, and protection, under the law. The movement aims to advance gender equality and to oppose sexual objectification.
metadata.Further information: Actress Lina Esco wanted to make a difference in the world all her life. Growing up dirt poor in Florida she vowed to one day campaign for equal rights for women in the US because she witnessed the struggles her mother had. To this day in the US women earn much less than men for equal work, they have glass ceilings in business and fewer opportunities in the corporate world. Women are earning the majority of undergraduate and graduate degrees (60 percent), while at the same time, women make up the majority of the poor in America. Surprisingly the U.S. Constitution does not guarantee equal rights for women. Since 1923, activists have been trying to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), which states, “Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.” However, ERA has never been passed and is not part of the Constitution. In addition, aspects of women's lives are also treated differently in many states in the US. For example, in Louisiana a woman can be arrested and jailed for breastfeeding in public. Lina had been acutely aware of the lack of equal rights for women and decided to put that in the spotlight, she decided on a novel approach and decided to use a metaphor that would have wide public impact. She decided on the nipple. In the US today, the nipples of men, that are no different from that of women can be sees and displayed in public, but female nipples not. They are considered indecent. This freedom men have in going topless was not always there. Until the 1930's men were prohibited from showing their nipples and were forced to wear swimwear that covered their nipples. They could be fined or jailed if they did not abide by the law. However, an organised protest in New York changed this for men. It was never extended to women. In this Lina saw a prime example of the lack of equal rights of women and decided to make a film called "Free the Nipple". She easily got money, shot it in New York City and completed the film in 2013. However, no film festival would take the film and she had trouble with distributors. While this was going on, word of the film came out and surprisingly a whole movement called "Free the Nipple" stared. The idea resonated with men and women across the US and became a social movement with annual celebrations and events across the country. This triggered interest in the film and it was released in 2014/15. American taboos surrounding the female nipple are further enforced by many social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram which prohibit any and all "graphic content" that pictures a woman's areola. Instagram's Community Guideline's demands of its users, "Keep your clothes on." However, this rule seems only to apply to images that contain women's nipples as they are promptly removed by Instagram unless the areola itself is covered. In contrast, photos featuring topless men are generally not subject to this regulation. Chelsea Handler, Miley Cyrus, Rihanna and Scout Willis have each received backlash from Instagram for sharing photos of their chests exposed. Willow Smith also had a post removed because it pictured her wearing a shirt with a pair of women's nipples printed on it, though the shirt itself was fairly conservative in cut. Some have even gone so far as to photoshop male nipples onto their pictures posted on Instagram in order to cover their female nipples. This is mostly used to make the comparison between the two and censorship. When explaining the need to remove nudity, Instagram's CEO Kevin Systrom blamed the rating system of Apple's app store. Eliminating online censorship of Free the Nipple posts is one of the goals of the movement. Censorship, and especially that of social media sites, exacerbates the problem that social movements, primarily those considered taboo, run into, which is spreading the message. The use of social media like Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram, has greatly improved activists ability to spread their message in the last decade, making it easier to create a collective identity. Free the Nipple activists need ICT's in their repertoire because social media shares lead to accelerated pluralism, which can then lead to the spillover effect, which can be seen in the Occupy Wall Street and Arab Spring movements. The spillover into the public sphere is what social movement activists hope for. In 2015, the campaign received attention in Iceland and was supported by MP Björt Ólafsdottir, who posted a topless photo of herself, in solidarity with a teenage activist who had received harassment for doing the same. Lina speaks exceptionally well, is articulate and passionate about her ideal for equal rights for women. We also have permission to use the film. The Free the Nipple website says: FREE THE NIPPLE IS A GLOBAL CAMPAIGN OF CHANGE, FOCUSED ON THE EQUALITY, EMPOWERMENT, AND FREEDOM OF ALL HUMAN BEINGS. FREE THE NIPPLE HAS BECOME A PREMIERE VOICE FOR GENDER EQUALITY, UTILIZING ALL FORMS OF MODERN MEDIA, TO RAISE AWARENESS AND EFFECT CHANGE ON VARIOUS SOCIAL ISSUES, AND INJUSTICES. WE BELIEVE THAT ALL HUMAN BEINGS ARE CREATED EQUAL. WE BELIEVE THAT THE TIME FOR CHANGE IS NOW. WE BELIEVE THAT TOGETHER, THROUGH ONE UNIFIED VOICE, WE CAN AFFECT CHANGE GLOBALLY. OUR MISSION: FREE THE NIPPLE IS A GLOBAL PLATFORM FOR CHANGE IN THE WORLD. WE BELIEVE THAT AS HUMAN BEINGS, WE SHOULD ALL BE TREATED EQUALLY. WE ARE A GLOBAL MOVEMENT OF EQUALITY, EMPOWERMENT AND FREEDOM. WE ARE A MOVEMENT OF CHANGE.
